learning.title: Quote a diff percentage for the rectangle the comparator compares, never the image
learning.trigger: Reading, quoting or reasoning about a visual-diff percentage from the UI parity gate (compare-paper.mjs, any specimen with a comparisonRegion), or judging whether a pinned baseline is "stale", "fine" or "a regression" from a pixel difference.
learning.mistake: Two distinct errors, both on the #248 sectionNavigation specimens. First: diffed the whole rendered PNG and reported the result as the gate's finding. The full 390x844 frame differs by 11.8%, which reads as a redesign of the whole page and would justify recapturing a Paper frame that must not be touched. The comparator only measures a declared sub-rectangle - 342x679 at offset (24,24), i.e. y 24..703 - and inside that rectangle the difference is 1187px = 0.511%, confined to two bands. The extra bands below y=703 (the grouped nav overflowing the frame) are outside the compared region and were never in scope. Second: having written that down, I then cropped with `d[24:703, 24:366]`, which already applies the offset, and added 24 again when writing the note - so it quoted absolute cosplaying as relative. QA measured the same pixels as y 636-646 and y 675-678 where the note said y 660-670 and y 699-702: identical pixel count, identical percentage, identical score, bands exactly 24px apart. I made this second error while writing the entry about measuring regions, which is exactly when the rule earns its place.
learning.rule: Before quoting any diff percentage, state the comparator's region: its offset and its dimensions. For a specimen baseline that is `comparisonRegion` in `docs/technical-design/ui-baselines/paper-baselines.json`; the gate reads exactly that rectangle and nothing else. A percentage without a stated rectangle is not a measurement, it is a guess about which pixels count.

When a whole-image and a region-only figure disagree, the region figure is the gate's verdict and the whole-image figure is context. Do not average them, and do not "explain" the gap as drift: compute both, say which is the verdict, and say what the difference outside the region is (here: content that renders below the compared rectangle, in the shipped design, not moved pixels inside it).

This has burned three times on the same specimen: twice by measuring full-frame (once pre-merge, once at the post-merge head), and once by double-counting the region offset. Treat the rectangle as part of the measurement's definition, not a detail to confirm afterwards.

State the frame AND check the offset is applied exactly once. "Region-relative" and "absolute" are different coordinate systems and a note must say which it uses. Cropping with `d[y:y+h, x:x+w]` already applies the offset, so indices from that array are region-relative - adding the offset again produces absolute-looking numbers for relative indices, and two careful people then report bands exactly 24px apart (the origin) while agreeing on every other number: same pixel count, same percentage, same score. Pick one frame, name it in the sentence that quotes the numbers, and when a count matches but a coordinate does not, suspect the frame before suspecting the measurement.

verification.requirement: A diff percentage is only reported alongside the region it was measured in (offset + width x height).
A "stale baseline" or "regression" conclusion names the bands that moved inside that region, and states that nothing else inside it moved.
When re-measuring at a new head, re-derive both figures rather than carrying a previous whole-image number forward.
Every band coordinate states its frame (region-relative or absolute) in the same sentence, and the offset is verified to have been applied exactly once.

learning.boundary: Measuring the full image is still correct when the question is "does anything anywhere differ" — e.g. deciding whether an unrelated area changed, or checking a render for clipping below the fold. The rule is about what a percentage is allowed to mean, not about which crops are ever legitimate.
